content_voiceover: This slide focuses on porphyria cutanea tarda, the porphyria you'll see most clinically. It's the most common porphyric disorder, about one in ten-thousand, from uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency, either inherited or, more often, acquired. Classic precipitating factors: sun exposure, alcohol, estrogen, excessive iron intake, and infections, especially hepatitis C, strongly associated with PCT. Patients develop a photosensitive bullous dermatosis on sun-exposed skin from circulating uroporphyrins causing photoactivated tissue damage, as seen in the blistering on the hand. Unlike AIP, PCT causes no neurovisceral attacks. Treatment starts with avoiding precipitating factors, sun protection, stopping alcohol and estrogen, treating hepatitis C. First-line treatment is repeated phlebotomy, which lowers hepatic iron stores, since iron promotes the oxidative damage that inhibits UROD. Low-dose hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine is an alternative, mobilizing and helping excrete hepatic porphyrins. Phlebotomy is the boards answer for PCT treatment.
keypoints: PCT = most common porphyria (1/10,000), UROD deficiency
Triggers: sun, alcohol, estrogen, iron, hepatitis C
Presentation: photosensitive bullous dermatosis, NO neurovisceral symptoms
keypoint_voiceover: Porphyria cutanea tarda is the most common porphyria, from UROD deficiency, triggered by sun, alcohol, estrogen, iron overload, and hepatitis C. It causes photosensitive bullous skin disease without neurovisceral symptoms, unlike AIP. First-line treatment is repeated phlebotomy to reduce hepatic iron; low-dose hydroxychloroquine or chloroquine is the alternative.
